profile.name: Yvette Armstrong
profile.summary: Hypertension - newly diagnosed, confused about sodium and salt
profile.background: Full-time state employee with an associate's degree in political science.
profile.persona: Curious, earnest, overwhelmed. Wants to understand but medical jargon loses her. Warms up when explanations use everyday words.
profile.source_notes: Recently diagnosed with Stage II hypertension (BP 155/110 mmHg), Yvette struggles to understand medical explanations and is confused about sodium and salt. BMI is 34. "My doctor told me, but I just didn't understand what she said." She needs clear education on what hypertension is, the role of sodium in blood pressure control, sodium limits, and the benefits of modest weight loss.
profile.provenance: Organizer CSV; demo case file data/cases/adult-yvette-armstrong.json

facts.label: Presenting concern
facts.record: Newly diagnosed Stage 2 hypertension at recent primary care visit. Referred for education on hypertension, sodium, and weight.
facts.patient_text: My doctor told me I have high blood pressure, hypertension she called it. Honestly, I left more confused than when I walked in.

facts.label: Work and home
facts.record: Full-time state employee; associate's degree in political science.
facts.patient_text: I work full time for the state. I have an associate's degree in political science, so I like to understand things - but medical words just lose me.

facts.label: Blood pressure and BMI
facts.record: BP 155/110 mmHg (Stage 2 hypertension range). BMI 34 (obesity class 1). Measurement dates not supplied.
facts.patient_text: At my last visit my blood pressure was 155 over 110, and they told me my BMI is 34.

facts.label: Sodium vs salt confusion
facts.record: Confused about the difference between sodium and salt.
facts.patient_text: That's the part that confuses me. Is sodium the same thing as salt? I hardly ever use the salt shaker, so I figured salt wasn't my problem.

facts.label: Understanding of diagnosis
facts.record: Did not understand the explanation given at diagnosis.
facts.patient_text: My doctor told me, but I just didn't understand what she said. She used a lot of words I didn't know, and I was too embarrassed to ask.

facts.record: Feels overwhelmed by the diagnosis and the number of changes.
facts.patient_text: Overwhelmed, mostly. Everyone keeps telling me to change everything at once, and I don't know where to start.

facts.record: Most weekday lunches from the work cafeteria; relies on canned soups and frozen dinners at home for convenience.
facts.patient_text: Most days I grab lunch in the cafeteria at work. At night I'm tired, so it's usually a canned soup or a frozen dinner.

facts.record: Willing to start with one or two concrete changes; prefers practical, step-by-step guidance.
facts.patient_text: I think I could start by checking labels on the soups I buy, and maybe walking at lunch. One or two things at a time.

reactions.patient_text: Yes, that's right. That's exactly where I am.
Okay. My blood pressure is too high, so my heart has to work harder. Salt has sodium in it, and I should keep sodium under 2,300 milligrams a day by reading labels. And canned soup is a big one.
Oh, so it's like too much pressure pushing on the pipes. Why didn't anyone say it like that before?
So salt has sodium in it, and the canned stuff is full of it even if I never touch the shaker. I had no idea.
I can do that. I'll look at the soup cans this weekend.
Just a few pounds makes a difference? That feels a lot more doable.
No, I think that covers it. This is the first time it actually made sense.
Okay. Home cuff, labels, and call if it's over 180 or I get chest pain. Thank you - really.

demo_script.clinician: Hello Ms. Armstrong, I'm a student clinician on your care team. Today I'd like to go over your recent diagnosis with you. What brings you in today?
What would you like me to call you?
Can you tell me about your work and home life?
What did your doctor tell you about your diagnosis?
That sounds really frustrating, and it makes sense that it was confusing. How do you feel about all of this?
Let's look at your numbers. Can you tell me your blood pressure reading and your BMI?
Tell me about what you usually eat in a typical day.
You mentioned canned soup. What do you know about salt and sodium?
Have you had any headaches, vision changes, chest pain, or dizziness?
demo_script.note: Not in the approved profile. The patient says so instead of inventing an answer - point this out to judges.

demo_script.clinician: Are you taking any medications right now, and do you have any allergies?
demo_script.note: Also not in the profile - second grounding moment.

demo_script.clinician: To summarize what I heard: your blood pressure is 155 over 110, which is stage 2 high blood pressure, and you'd like to understand salt and sodium better.
Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. When it stays high, your heart works harder.
Salt contains sodium, and sodium raises blood pressure because your body holds on to extra water. Try to keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day - canned soups and frozen dinners are often very high.
Checking the nutrition facts label is the easiest way to spot sodium, and fresh foods with herbs and spices are great swaps.
What feels realistic for you to start with?
Just to make sure I explained it well, can you tell me back in your own words what we talked about?
Is there anything else you'd like to ask?

Our next step is to check your blood pressure at home with a cuff, and we'll follow up in two weeks. If you see a reading over 180, or have chest pain or vision changes, call 911 or go to the emergency room. I'll discuss this plan with my supervisor.

intentional_gaps: Does not ask about family history or other conditions (U-INFO-4) - shows up as a gap in feedback.
Does not explain the benefit of modest weight loss (YA-D4) - shows up as a next-attempt suggestion.
Optional live improvisation: add 'Losing even a small amount of weight, about 5%, can lower your blood pressure.' before step 15 to show the score go up.
